lesson.title: Solid, Liquid, Gas, or Dissolved: Labeling the Players in a Reaction
lesson.summary: State symbols, written in parentheses after each formula in a chemical equation, record the physical state of every reactant and product, adding detail a bare formula cannot show on its own.
lesson.body:
A balanced Chemical Equation correctly identifies every substance involved in a reaction and correctly accounts for every atom, but by itself it leaves out something a chemist standing at the bench would notice immediately: what physical form each substance is actually in. Is a product a gas that bubbles away, a solid that settles out, or simply dissolved in the surrounding water? Recall from States of Matter that a given substance can exist as a solid, liquid, or gas depending on conditions; chemical equations capture which of those states applies to each substance at the moment of reaction using a short label called a state symbol, written in parentheses immediately after the formula.

There are four standard state symbols. (s) marks a solid, (l) marks a pure liquid, and (g) marks a gas. The fourth, (aq), stands for aqueous and marks a substance dissolved in water; it is a distinct category from (l) because an aqueous substance is not a pure liquid on its own; it is a solute dissolved in a solvent, tying directly back to what you already know from Solutions. Writing NaCl(aq) says specifically that the sodium chloride is dissolved in water, not sitting as a dry solid crystal, and that distinction can completely change how, or whether, a reaction proceeds.

Consider a classic precipitation reaction, written with full state symbols: NaCl(aq) + AgNO3(aq) -> NaNO3(aq) + AgCl(s). Both reactants start out dissolved in water, invisible as separate ions swimming through solution, which is exactly what the (aq) labels communicate. But one of the possible products, silver chloride, does not dissolve in water, so as soon as Ag+ and Cl- ions encounter each other, they lock together into a solid that separates out of the solution as a visible white precipitate, marked (s). The other product, sodium nitrate, stays fully dissolved, marked (aq). Nothing about the bare formulas NaCl, AgNO3, NaNO3, and AgCl tells you that a solid is about to appear out of a clear liquid; the state symbols are what capture that. As a check, this equation is already balanced with every coefficient equal to 1: the left side has one Na, one Cl, one Ag, one N, and three O, and the right side has exactly the same count, one Na, one N, three O, one Ag, and one Cl.

State symbols also flag when a gas is released, which is often the most visually obvious sign that a reaction is happening. A preview of a pattern you will study in the Decomposition Reactions chapter is CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g): solid calcium carbonate breaking down into solid calcium oxide and gaseous carbon dioxide, which physically bubbles or streams away, permanently leaving the reaction mixture. Learning to read state symbols is a small addition to the grammar of a chemical equation, but it is what turns a bare list of formulas into a genuine description of what an observer would actually see happen in the lab.
